A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-GS research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across appendix reordering and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original Karel and Karel-Hard evaluations, language and search ablations, and LLM revision experiments in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds PATHFOLLOW and WALLAVOIDER evaluations and a GPT-4 knowledge probe.

M1.justification: Task-aware prompting, Pythonic-DSL generation, conversion and post-processing, and Scheduled Hill Climbing remain unchanged. The scheduler equations and detailed prompts match across versions. Expanded explanations of domain knowledge describe components already documented in v1.

E1.justification: v2 retains all ten original tasks and adds PATHFOLLOW and WALLAVOIDER (Section 5.4; Appendix C.3). These introduce constrained marker-path following and interior-cell marker placement, providing a bounded expansion within the existing Karel domain.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain LEAPS, HPRL, CEBS, and HC. Search, language-generation, initialization, and revision comparisons also retain their methods. The added tasks reuse HC as the comparator; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: Appendix G adds a testing procedure that supplies two paper titles and asks GPT-4 to enumerate their benchmark tasks. The added task evaluations hold domain/DSL prompts and hyperparameters fixed. Existing experiments retain 32 task variants, the one-million-program budget, and their reported search settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds checks of extensibility with unchanged shared prompts and a GPT-4 recall case study investigating possible benchmark memorization (Section 5.4; Appendix G). Existing language, search, initialization, and revision analyses remain intact. These are focused supplementary checks.

E5.justification: Both versions report 32 seeds for LLM-GS and HC, five for other main baselines, eight for language ablations, and five for revision experiments. Existing uncertainty displays remain unchanged, and v2 introduces no new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 8 adds results showing LLM-GS outperforming HC on both new tasks. Figure 4(d) revises the CEBS TOPOFF curve; the other nine panels and Table 3 are unchanged. Appendices G and H additionally report unsuccessful task recall and aggregated benchmark performance.

T1.justification: The scheduler equations, DSL grammar, and mathematical treatment are retained, including the scheduler appendix moved from A to E. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2 adds no formal theorem, derivation, or revised mathematical assumption.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit claim that users without programming or domain/DSL knowledge can obtain effective policies for new tasks through natural-language descriptions. The original sample-efficiency, Pythonic-DSL, and Scheduled Hill Climbing contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendices A and J substantially expand applicability boundaries, including expert preparation of new domains, suitable DSLs, and difficulty with low-level control. Appendix G newly argues that improvements reflect reasoning rather than memorization and claims to exclude leakage. The main text also removes the interpretation that supplying more revision feedback necessarily works best.

D1.justification: v2 specifies gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09, identifies Carvalho et al.'s LEAPS reimplementation, and documents the new task descriptions and knowledge-probe prompt. These clarify reproducibility without establishing an implementation change. However, Section 5.1 drops v1's explicit statement that initialization uses 32 programs.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning relative to RL sample-efficiency techniques, library-learning program synthesis, and alternative interpretable policy representations. It adds relevant literature and explicitly discusses orthogonality to other efficiency methods and limits across policy representations, beyond the retained related-work discussion.

P1.justification: Section 4.1 is rewritten to distinguish domain knowledge from task descriptions, and the concluding section becomes Discussion. Existing appendices are reordered, citations change to author-year style, and wording is polished. Most retained methodological prose and detailed prompts remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn to illustrate scheduled iterations. v2 adds task-performance plots, task illustrations, GPT-4 prompt/response displays, and an aggregate plot. It also changes title, heading, and header styling and substantially redistributes existing figures and tables throughout the document.

improvement.justification: The new tasks provide useful evidence of extensibility within Karel, while expanded limitations, research positioning, and implementation attribution improve the paper's clarity and scope. Gains are incremental over v1's existing experimental foundation. The leakage probe does not justify conclusively excluding memorization, and removing the explicit initialization size slightly weakens reproducibility.
